title: Tides
standard_code: Grade 8, Quarter 3: Earth and Space Science
standard_text: Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity and partly by the Sun's; there are usually two high and two low tides a day; spring tides and neap tides depend on the positions of the Sun and Moon; tides affect coastal life and activities. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 8, Quarter 3: Earth and Space Science)
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 3: Earth and Space Science): high and low tides, the Moon's gravity, spring and neap tides, eclipses and the Moon, and tides in coastal life. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Spring tides happen at new moon and full moon.
body_html:
How to think about it

The Moon's gravity pulls on the Earth's oceans, making them bulge on the side facing the Moon and on the opposite side. As the Earth rotates, a coast passes through two bulges, so there are usually two high tides and two low tides each day.

When the Sun, Earth and Moon are in line (new moon and full moon), their pulls add up and give spring tides with the largest tidal range. When they are at right angles (quarter moons), the tides are smaller: neap tides. Fishers, boat operators and coastal communities plan around tides.

Example

Which phase gives spring tides?

Sun, Earth, Moon in line

Answer: new moon or full moon

Example

How many high tides a day?

Two bulges

Answer: usually two

Common mistakes

  • Thinking tides are caused by wind.
  • Thinking spring tides only happen in spring.
  • Thinking the Sun has no effect on tides.

faq.q: Why does the Moon affect tides more than the Sun?
faq.a: It is much closer to the Earth.

faq.q: Why do mangroves matter on tidal coasts?
faq.a: They protect the shore from waves and storm surges and shelter young fish.

items.q: Why does the Moon seem to change shape?
c: Earth's shadow covers part of it every night.
We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth.
items.e: These are the phases of the Moon.

items.q: Christian photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with waxing crescent. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon.

items.q: What is a high tide?
c: when the sea water is coldest
when the sea level is highest along the shore
when the Moon is not in the sky
items.e: At high tide water comes farther up the beach.

items.q: What is a neap tide?
c: a tide with the smallest difference between high and low tide, at the quarter moons
the highest tide of the year
a tide caused by a typhoon
items.e: The Sun and Moon pull at right angles.

items.q: How many high tides does a coast usually have each day?
items.e: There are usually two high tides and two low tides each day.

items.q: Diane photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with first quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: first quarter → full moon → third quarter → new moon.

items.q: Dennis reads: “The Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on Earth.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: What happens in a lunar eclipse?
c: The Sun hides behind Earth's clouds.
Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
items.e: The Moon can look red.

items.q: Rose photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with full moon. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: full moon → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Joy reads: “Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: Why does the Moon affect tides more than the Sun?
c: the Moon is much closer to the Earth
the Moon is bigger than the Sun
items.e: Distance matters a lot for tides.

items.q: Which direction does the Sun appear to rise?
items.e: Earth spins from west to east.

items.q: How long does Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
items.e: That is why we have years.

items.q: Why do fishers in coastal villages check the tide?
c: tides affect when boats can leave and where fish and shellfish can be found
tides tell the time of earthquakes
tides show the color of the sea
items.e: Many people gather shellfish at low tide.

items.q: Nico reads: “The Moon turns a reddish color for over an hour, and everyone on the night side of Earth can see it.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Kenneth photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with waning crescent. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waning crescent → new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter.

items.q: What is a low tide?
c: when there are no waves at all
when the sea level is lowest along the shore
items.e: At low tide more of the beach can be seen.

items.q: What causes ocean tides?
c: mainly the Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's water
items.e: Two high tides a day happen in most places.

items.q: Kevin photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with first quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous.

items.q: Rafael reads: “People in a narrow path on Earth see the Sun's disk completely covered for a few minutes.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: Hazel photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with waning crescent. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waning crescent → waxing crescent → waxing gibbous → waning gibbous.

items.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
c: The Moon rotates once in the same time it takes to orbit Earth.
items.e: Synchronous rotation.

items.q: Which statement about tides is correct?
c: the oceans bulge on the side facing the Moon and on the opposite side
only the side facing the Moon has high tide
items.e: That is why there are two high tides a day.

items.q: Jomar photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with waxing crescent. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waxing crescent → waxing gibbous → waning gibbous → waning crescent.

items.q: What happens in a solar eclipse?
c: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and blocks the Sun.
items.e: Never look at the Sun, even during an eclipse.

items.q: Why is it dangerous to walk far out on a beach at low tide?
c: the tide may come back quickly and cut you off
items.e: Always check tide times.

items.q: Which is a benefit of tides?
c: they can be used to make electricity (tidal energy)
they make the sea fresh water
items.e: Moving water can turn turbines.

items.q: Mangrove areas are flooded at high tide and exposed at low tide. Why are mangroves important?
c: they block sunlight from the sea
they protect coasts from waves and storm surges and are nurseries for fish
items.e: Mangrove roots trap mud and break waves.

items.q: Kenneth photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with waning gibbous. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waning gibbous → waning crescent → waxing crescent → waxing gibbous.

items.q: Emmanuel reads: “The Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on Earth.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: Why do we see the same side of the Moon all the time?
c: The other side is dark forever.
The Moon spins once for each orbit of Earth.
items.e: This is called being tidally locked.

items.q: What happens to the sea level at the moment of a full moon?
c: the tide stops for a day
items.e: The Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line.

items.q: Arnel photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with third quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: third quarter → waning crescent → new moon → waxing crescent.

items.q: Angel reads: “People in a narrow path on Earth see the Sun's disk completely covered for a few minutes.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: About how long is it from one high tide to the next?
items.e: Tides come about 50 minutes later each day.

items.q: Trisha reads: “Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
c: the 23.5° tilt of Earth's axis as Earth orbits the Sun
items.e: Tilt changes the angle of sunlight.

items.q: What is the tidal range?
c: the difference in height between high tide and low tide
items.e: The tidal range is largest at spring tides.

items.q: Rose reads: “The Moon turns a reddish color for over an hour, and everyone on the night side of Earth can see it.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: Which Moon phases bring neap tides?
items.e: The Sun and Moon pull at right angles.

items.q: Rose sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.q: Tonight Kristine sees a waxing gibbous. Which phase came just before it?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.e: New: no lit side visible. Full: the whole face is lit.

items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the first quarter?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Tonight Vincent sees a third quarter. About which phase will Vincent see one week later?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waxing crescent?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: What causes day and night?
items.e: One rotation takes about 24 hours.

items.q: Tonight Patricia sees a third quarter. Which phase came just before it?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Tonight Bryan sees a new moon. Which phase came just before it?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the last quarter?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waxing gibbous?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Miguel sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: New: no lit side visible. Full: the whole face is lit.

items.q: Nico sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.q: Tonight Kenneth sees a first quarter. About which phase will Kenneth see about two weeks later?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Tonight Renz sees a waning gibbous. Which phase comes next?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Why are shadows shortest at noon?
c: The Sun is highest in the sky.
It is always cloudy at noon.
The Sun is lowest in the sky.
items.e: High Sun, short shadow.

items.q: Vincent photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with full moon. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: full moon → third quarter → new moon → first quarter.

items.q: Lance photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with new moon. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the new moon?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Carmela photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with waxing gibbous. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waxing gibbous → waning gibbous → waning crescent → waxing crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the new moon?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the first quarter?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Sheila photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with new moon. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: new moon → first quarter → full moon → third quarter.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waxing gibbous?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waning crescent?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Why is it unsafe to look directly at a solar eclipse without eclipse glasses?
c: Sunlight can damage your eyes even when most of the Sun is covered.
items.e: Use proper eye protection.

items.q: Is the far side of the Moon always dark?
c: No. It gets sunlight too; we just never see it from Earth.
items.e: It is fully lit at new moon.

items.q: What causes the seasons?
c: Earth's tilted axis as it orbits the Sun
items.e: The tilt changes how directly sunlight reaches each place.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the full moon?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waning gibbous?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: About how many days after a new moon is the next full moon?
items.e: A full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days, so opposite phases are about half that apart.

items.q: Rodel photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with waning gibbous. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent → new moon.

items.q: How long does the Moon take to go through all its phases?
items.e: The word month comes from Moon.

items.q: Arnel photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with third quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: third quarter → new moon → first quarter → full moon.

items.q: Why should you never look straight at a solar eclipse?
c: The Sun's light can permanently damage your eyes.
items.e: Use eclipse glasses or a pinhole viewer.

items.q: What does a sundial use to tell time?
c: the shadow made by the Sun
items.e: Shadows move as Earth rotates.

Why do astronauts weigh less on the Moon?
c: There is no gravity on the Moon.
The Moon's gravity is weaker because it has less mass than the Earth.
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: Gravitational field strength on the Earth is 10 N/kg. What is the weight there of an object with a mass of 40 kg?
items.e: weight = mass × g = 40 × 10 = 400 N.

items.q: Gravitational field strength on the Earth is 10 N/kg. What is the weight there of an object with a mass of 50 kg?
items.e: weight = mass × g = 50 × 10 = 500 N.

items.q: On Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg), Emmanuel's backpack weighs 185 N. What is its mass?
items.e: mass = weight ÷ g = 185 ÷ 3.7 = 50 kg.

items.q: On Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg), Rafael's backpack weighs 222 N. What is its mass?
items.e: mass = weight ÷ g = 222 ÷ 3.7 = 60 kg.

items.q: What is mass?
c: the amount of matter in an object
the force of gravity on it
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.e: weight = mass × g = 45 × 25 = 1,125 N.
